source.title: On the Algorithmic Stability and Generalization of Adaptive Optimization Methods
source.authors: H. Nguyen; Hai Pham; Sashank J. Reddi; Barnabás Póczos

record.tranche_reason: The study measures training–test loss gaps after changing adaptive-optimizer settings and adding AdamW weight decay, using synthetic and CIFAR-10 tasks.
record.gate_note: The study reports generalization-gap outcomes for optimizer settings. Its comparisons are between Adam and Adagrad or AdamW, not SGD; results about parameter distance and train or test loss alone are not separately recorded as claim-version results.
record.test_reason: The study measures algorithmic stability and absolute train–test loss gaps while comparing adaptive optimizers and varying β2 or weight decay. V4 concerns held-out performance relative to SGD and recovery of that performance through recipe changes. There is no SGD comparison, and a smaller train–test gap alone does not establish better held-out performance or recovery to SGD. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors derive conditional stability and generalization bounds for adaptive methods without first-moment momentum, emphasize dependence on β2, and show that suitably chosen AdamW parameters yield an iteration-independent stability bound. They interpret the synthetic and CIFAR-10 experiments as supporting their theory; empirical weight-decay comparisons are confined to the synthetic tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Measures train–test loss gaps and parameter distances while varying adaptive-optimizer settings and AdamW weight decay; it does not reproduce the cited SGD-versus-adaptive benchmark recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported generalization gap changes with Adam β2; AdamW has lower gaps than Adam in the two synthetic tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: On the two synthetic tasks, the authors report that Adagrad's train–test loss gap grows more slowly than Adam's, using the same or a larger initial learning rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adagrad can exhibit slower growth of the absolute train–test loss gap than fixed-β2 Adam in small synthetic overfitting tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing fixed β2 reduces the reported absolute train–test loss gap in synthetic classification, synthetic regression, and CIFAR-10 VGG11. For CIFAR-10, the text also reports improvements in both training and test losses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive-optimizer generalization gaps and held-out losses can depend strongly on β2 in the tested configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: AdamW has smaller absolute train–test loss gaps than Adam on both synthetic tasks, with weight decay 5.0 for classification and 1.0 for regression and β1 = 0, β2 = 0.999.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoupled weight decay can reduce Adam's train–test loss gap in small synthetic overfitting tasks.

record.code_released: not stated (supplementary material says code will be publicly released)
record.problems: The empirical tasks are small synthetic datasets and one CIFAR-10 VGG11 setup; each setting uses 20 trials. The numerical outcomes are presented in figures without extractable values in the supplied text. No SGD comparison is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Parameter-distance and train-loss/test-loss trajectories were not included because they do not themselves measure the train–test gap or a V4 comparison. Figure 1's Adagrad-only gap trajectory was omitted because no comparator is shown and its direction is described as growth; Figures 3 and 5's β2 settings are retained as figure-only rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

Adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance under limited tuning; broader tuning; recovery through decoupled weight decay or optimizer switching; language-model comparisons. Smaller synthetic train–test gaps with AdamW do not establish the stated recovery.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout effects, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures. Dataset-replacement stability is a different construct.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and measuring test accuracy after retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are relative to the supplied claim versions. cannot_determine does not negate the authors' explicit directional findings, which are retained under fits_no_version. Exact curve values cannot be recovered from the supplied text. References to SGD's advantages are background citations, not this study's results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization.

No SGD or momentum-SGD comparison, language benchmark, limited-tuning comparison, broader-tuning comparison, or optimizer switch. Tests Adam versus AdamW under weight decay and reports Adam versus Adagrad and Adam β2 settings.
Large versus small batch at fixed epoch budgets and batch-size adaptation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: synthetic classification and regression with AdamW versus Adam
reader_labels.reason: AdamW has lower reported generalization error than Adam in both tasks (R23, R25). This supports the weight-decay qualification stated in V4, but does not test recovery to SGD performance.
